events.title: Early Civilization Settlement
events.description: Agricultural settlements began appearing in Bolivian highlands. Early inhabitants domesticated llamas and alpacas, and cultivated high-altitude crops like potatoes and quinoa. Lake Titicaca region became important cultural center, where agricultural innovations laid foundation for later civilizations.

events.title: Chiripa Culture
events.description: Chiripa culture developed on southern shore of Lake Titicaca, one of Bolivia's first complex societies. Chiripa people built stone temples and ritual centers, developed sophisticated pottery and textile techniques. This culture was precursor to later Tiwanaku civilization.

events.title: Pucara Culture Influence
events.description: Pucara culture from northern Lake Titicaca shore in Peru began influencing Bolivian highlands. Pucara architectural styles, religious imagery and pottery traditions spread to Bolivian region, promoting trans-lake cultural exchange and trade.

events.title: National Revolution
events.description: Armed uprising erupted in La Paz, MNR militia, miners and police fought army for three days. Revolutionaries seized arsenals, armed populace. Army finally surrendered, Paz Estenssoro returned from exile to assume presidency. 1952 revolution was one of 20th century Latin America's most important social revolutions, alongside Mexican and Cuban revolutions. About 600 died in fighting.

events.title: Tiwanaku Civilization Rise
events.description: Tiwanaku civilization rose on southern shore of Lake Titicaca, becoming one of Andes' most important pre-Columbian civilizations. Tiwanaku city developed as religious and political center, with massive stone architecture, sophisticated agricultural systems and advanced hydraulic engineering. City population at peak may have reached 40-50 thousand.

events.title: Tiwanaku Expansion
events.description: Tiwanaku civilization entered expansion period, influence extending from southern Peruvian coast to northern Chile and northwestern Argentina. Tiwanaku established trade networks, exchanging highland products (like freeze-dried potatoes, alpaca wool) with coastal regions' fish, shells and coca leaves. Tiwanaku's religious and artistic styles had far-reaching influence.

events.title: Tiwanaku Golden Age
events.description: Tiwanaku reached civilization peak. Monumental architecture like Gateway of the Sun, Akapana Pyramid and Puma Punku built during this period. Tiwanaku developed complex agricultural systems, including raised fields (suka kollus) to resist frost. Sophisticated astronomical observations and calendar systems controlled agricultural activities. Population may have reached hundreds of thousands.

events.title: Tiwanaku Decline
events.description: Tiwanaku civilization began declining, possibly due to prolonged drought and climate change causing agricultural failure. City gradually abandoned, population dispersed. Tiwanaku's collapse led Andean highlands into fragmentation period, with multiple small kingdoms competing for power.

events.title: Post-Tiwanaku Period
events.description: After Tiwanaku's decline, Bolivian highlands saw multiple regional kingdoms emerge, including Aymara-speaking Qolla, Lupaca, Pacajes and Caranga. These kingdoms controlled different ecological zones from highlands to valleys, establishing vertical trade networks. They built hilltop fortresses (pukaras) for defense against enemies.

events.title: Inca Empire Expansion Begins
events.description: Inca Empire under Pachacuti began large-scale expansion. Inca armies advanced southward, beginning conquest of Bolivian highlands' Aymara kingdoms. Incas used combination of military conquest and diplomatic marriage to gradually incorporate Bolivia into Tawantinsuyu (Inca Empire).

events.title: Aymara Kingdoms Conquest
events.description: Inca Empire under Pachacuti and son Tupac Inca Yupanqui conquered Aymara kingdoms around Lake Titicaca. Qolla and Lupaca kingdoms submitted after fierce resistance. Incas incorporated local elites into imperial administration, but also forcibly relocated populations (mitma system) to prevent rebellion. Aymara language and culture were preserved.

events.title: Qullasuyu Establishment
events.description: Bolivian highlands became core of Qullasuyu ('Land of the South'), one of Inca Empire's four administrative regions. Incas established administrative centers at important sites like Tiwanaku, Copacabana and near Oruro. Inca road system connected highlands with Cusco and other imperial regions.

events.title: Chiquitano and Moxos Region Resistance
events.description: Incas attempted to conquer eastern lowlands' Chiquitano and Moxos regions but met fierce resistance from forest tribes. Tropical rainforest environment, diseases and guerrilla warfare tactics made lasting Inca control difficult. Eastern lowlands largely remained independent from Inca Empire.

events.title: Inca Civil War
events.description: After Inca emperor Huayna Capac's death, sons Huascar and Atahualpa fought civil war for throne. Qullasuyu's Aymara troops mainly supported Huascar. Civil war severely weakened Inca Empire, creating opportunity for Spanish conquest. Atahualpa won in 1532 but was captured by Spanish same year.

events.title: Spanish Conquest Begins
events.description: Francisco Pizarro captured Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, beginning Spanish conquest of Inca Empire. Though conquest mainly occurred in Peru, news and impact quickly reached Bolivian highlands. Local Inca rulers and Aymara nobles reacted variedly to Spanish invasion.

events.title: Spanish Army Enters Bolivia
events.description: Diego de Almagro led Spanish expedition across Bolivian highlands to Chile. This was first Spanish military force to formally enter present-day Bolivia. Almagro's power struggle with Pizarro extended to this region, causing internal conflicts among Spanish conquerors.

events.title: Chuquisaca Founded
events.description: Spanish founded Chuquisaca city (modern Sucre) in highland valley with mild climate suitable for Europeans. Chuquisaca became main Spanish city and administrative center of Alto Perú (colonial name for Bolivian region), also center of Church power.

events.title: Potosí Silver Discovery
events.description: Massive silver deposits discovered at Cerro Rico mountain in Potosí, changing Bolivian and global history. Legend says Indian shepherd discovered silver. After news spread, thousands of Spanish and Indians rushed in. Potosí rapidly grew into one of Americas' largest and richest cities, population reaching about 160,000 by early 17th century, exceeding contemporary London and Paris.

events.title: La Paz Founded
events.description: Spanish captain Alonso de Mendoza founded La Paz city (Nuestra Señora de La Paz, 'Our Lady of Peace') in highland valley, commemorating end of civil war among Spanish conquerors. La Paz's strategic location between Cusco and Potosí made it important trade and transportation center. City in deep valley enjoyed relatively mild climate.

events.title: Chuquisaca Diocese Established
events.description: Pope Paul IV established Chuquisaca Diocese (later elevated to Archdiocese), responsible for Catholic affairs in Alto Perú. Church became core pillar of colonial society, controlling education, charity and moral supervision. Missionaries systematically evangelized Indians, though many indigenous beliefs secretly continued.

events.title: Toledo Viceregal Reforms
events.description: Peruvian Viceroy Francisco de Toledo implemented comprehensive reforms profoundly affecting Alto Perú. Toledo established reducciones, forcing Indians to concentrate for control and taxation. He reorganized mita system, forcibly conscripting Indian labor to Potosí and other silver mines. These reforms made Spanish colonial rule more efficient but had devastating impact on Indian population.

events.title: Last Inca Emperor Executed
events.description: Viceroy Toledo captured Vilcabamba, imprisoned last Inca resister Túpac Amaru I, and executed him in Cusco. This marked official end of Inca dynasty, though Inca legacy and culture continued in Andean region including Bolivia. Many Aymara and Quechua nobles continued serving local positions in colonial system.

events.title: Potosí Mint Established
events.description: Spanish established Royal Mint (Casa de la Moneda) in Potosí, minting extracted silver into coins on site. Mint used Indian laborers and African slaves, producing coins circulating globally. Potosí silver greatly enriched Spanish crown but also triggered European inflation. Mint building preserved today as important museum.

events.title: Potosí Silver Peak
events.description: Potosí silver production reached peak, becoming world's largest silver producer. City population exceeded 150,000, with 36 churches, numerous taverns and theaters. Potosí had famous saying: 'worth a Potosí' (valer un Potosí) meaning priceless. However silver mining's cost was deaths of tens of thousands of Indian and African laborers, especially under mita forced labor system.

events.title: Jesuit Missions Established
events.description: Jesuits began establishing missions (Reducciones) in Bolivia's eastern lowlands, particularly in Chiquitano and Moxos regions. Jesuit priests protected Indians from slave raiders while teaching Christianity, music and European agricultural techniques. These missions developed unique musical tradition combining Baroque music with indigenous elements. Mission architecture preserved today, listed as World Heritage sites.

events.title: University of San Francisco Xavier Founded
events.description: University of San Francisco Xavier established in Chuquisaca, one of Americas' oldest universities. University trained colonial elite, including criollos (Spanish descendants born in Americas) and some mestizos and Indian nobles. University became center for Enlightenment thought dissemination, later training many independence movement leaders.

events.title: Copacabana Virgin Cult
events.description: Black Virgin of Copacabana became Andes' most important pilgrimage center. This cult combined pre-Columbian Lake Titicaca's sacred status with Catholic Virgin Mary faith. Thousands of pilgrims annually visit Copacabana, tradition continuing today. Syncretism prevalent in Bolivian religious life.

events.title: Bourbon Reform Eve
events.description: Spanish Bourbon dynasty replaced Habsburg dynasty, beginning reforms in American colonies. Alto Perú in late 17th century faced declining silver production, population decrease and economic stagnation. Colonial elites began resenting Madrid's heavy-handed policies, sowing seeds for future independence movement.

events.title: Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata Established
events.description: Spain established Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata with capital in Buenos Aires. Alto Perú (Bolivia) transferred from Viceroyalty of Lima to new Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata. This changed trade routes and administrative connections, Potosí silver now exported more through Buenos Aires than Lima. This change influenced border demarcation after independence.

events.title: Túpac Amaru II Rebellion
events.description: Túpac Amaru II from Cusco, Peru led massive Indian rebellion against Spanish colonial rule. Rebellion quickly spread to Alto Perú, particularly Lake Titicaca region. Aymara leaders like Túpac Katari and Bartolina Sisa led rebellion in Bolivia, besieging La Paz for months. Rebellion brutally suppressed, leaders executed, but it demonstrated Indian resistance spirit.

events.title: La Paz Siege
events.description: Aymara leader Túpac Katari led 40,000 Indian army besieging La Paz, cutting off food and supplies. Spanish and criollos in city faced famine, thousands died. Siege lasted 109 days, one of colonial period's most intense Indian resistances. Eventually Spanish reinforcements broke siege, Túpac Katari captured and drawn and quartered, becoming Bolivian resistance symbol.

events.title: Chuquisaca Revolution
events.description: Criollos in Chuquisaca launched coup, overthrowing Spanish viceroy and establishing autonomous government junta. This was one of Latin American independence movement's earliest uprisings, predating Buenos Aires and other regions. Revolutionaries claimed loyalty to imprisoned Spanish King Ferdinand VII but actually sought autonomy. Uprising suppressed by Peruvian viceroy's troops months later.

events.title: La Paz Revolution
events.description: Inspired by Chuquisaca, criollos and mestizos in La Paz launched uprising, establishing autonomous government junta. Revolutionary leader Pedro Domingo Murillo issued radical manifesto declaring: 'We have kept silent long enough...now is time to break chains!' Uprising also quickly suppressed, leaders executed. 1809 called Bolivian independence movement's 'First Cry.'

events.title: Independence War
events.description: Alto Perú became battlefield for prolonged intense fighting between Spanish royalists and independentists. Buenos Aires sent multiple expeditions attempting to liberate Alto Perú, all failed. Guerrilla forces (republiquetas) harassed Spanish troops in rural areas, led by local leaders like Manuel Ascencio Padilla and Juana Azurduy. War caused enormous casualties and economic destruction, particularly Potosí silver mining nearly stopped.

events.title: Battle of Ayacucho
events.description: Simón Bolívar's lieutenant Antonio José de Sucre defeated Spanish royalist army at Ayacucho, Peru, effectively ending Spanish rule in South America. This opened way for Alto Perú's liberation. Sucre then led army into Alto Perú, welcomed by people.

events.title: Bolivian Independence
events.description: Assembly meeting in Chuquisaca declared Alto Perú independent, establishing Republic of Bolivia named after liberator Simón Bolívar. Antonio José de Sucre elected first president. New nation faced enormous challenges: economic bankruptcy, racial divisions, regional conflicts and lack of political experience. August 6 became Bolivian national day.

events.title: Bolivarian Constitution
events.description: Simón Bolívar drafted constitution for Bolivia, establishing strong presidential system with lifetime presidency. Constitution envisioned Peru-Bolivia federation, but this plan never realized. Bolívar's authoritarian constitutional ideas sparked controversy in Bolivia, President Sucre attempted implementing reforms but faced strong opposition.

events.title: Sucre Resignation and Political Turmoil
events.description: Facing rebellion and assassination attempts, President Sucre resigned and left Bolivia. Peruvian army invaded, occupying La Paz. Bolivia descended into chaos, beginning century-long cycle of political instability and military coups. In 19th century, Bolivia experienced nearly 200 coups or coup attempts, average presidential term under 2 years.

events.title: Santa Cruz Presidency and Confederation
events.description: General Andrés de Santa Cruz became Bolivia's most stable early ruler. He promoted modernization, reformed laws and education, stabilized economy. In 1836 he established Peru-Bolivia Confederation, briefly unifying two nations. But Chile and Argentina opposed confederation, Chile defeated confederation army at Yungay battle in 1839, confederation dissolved. This defeat opened new round of chaos.

events.title: Battle of Ingavi
events.description: Bolivian President José Ballivián defeated invading Peruvian army at Battle of Ingavi, important victory in Bolivian military history. Ballivián became national hero, symbolizing Bolivia's survival and sovereignty. However this victory couldn't mask continued internal political turmoil.

events.title: Silver Mining Revival
events.description: New silver discoveries and technological improvements, particularly in Huanuni and Oruro mining areas, brought silver mining revival. Silver barons like Gregorio Pacheco and Aniceto Arce accumulated enormous wealth. These silver oligarchs controlled politics, establishing so-called 'Conservative oligarchy rule,' governing Bolivia until early 20th century. Economic growth mainly benefited small elite, most Indians and mestizos remained poor.

events.title: War of the Pacific
events.description: Bolivia and Peru fought War of the Pacific against Chile over nitrate-rich Atacama Desert. War was catastrophic for Bolivia: Chilean army occupied Bolivia's entire coastal province including Antofagasta port. 1884 truce agreement made Bolivia lose Pacific Ocean access, becoming landlocked. This loss became trauma in Bolivian national consciousness, Bolivia still demands sea access restoration.

events.title: Federal Revolution and Capital Move
events.description: La Paz's Liberal Party launched Federal Revolution against Chuquisaca Conservative oligarchy rule. La Paz's economic and population growth enabled it to challenge traditional capital's status. After civil war Liberals won, government seat moved to La Paz, though Chuquisaca retained nominal constitutional capital status. This reflected economic transformation of rising tin mining, mainly near La Paz.

events.title: Tin Mining Boom
events.description: Bolivia became world's major tin producer, tin replacing silver as main export commodity. Three tin barons: Simón Patiño, Mauricio Hochschild and Carlos Aramayo controlled economy, called 'Tin Barons.' Patiño became one of world's richest men, but most wealth flowed abroad. Tin miners labored in harsh conditions, miners' movement began organizing.

events.title: Acre Territory Loss
events.description: Bolivia after conflict with Brazil signed Treaty of Petrópolis, ceding rubber-rich Acre region to Brazil in exchange for £2 million compensation and railway construction promise. This was Bolivia's another major territorial loss after Pacific coast. Bolivia barely benefited from rubber boom, territorial loss deepened national humiliation feelings.

events.title: Miners' Movement Rise
events.description: Tin miners began organizing unions, demanding better wages and working conditions. Harsh mine conditions (silicosis, accidents, low wages) sparked radicalism. Miners' movement influenced by anarchist and socialist ideas. Government and mine owners responded with repression and occasional concessions. Miners' movement became Bolivia's most important social force in 20th century.

events.title: Chaco War
events.description: Bolivia fought Chaco War against Paraguay over Gran Chaco region, believed rich in oil. War was disaster for Bolivia: despite population and economic advantages, Bolivian army suffered terrible defeat in jungle warfare, about 65,000 Bolivians died. By 1935 armistice, Bolivia lost three-quarters of disputed territory. War exposed government corruption and incompetence, sparked revolutionary sentiment.

events.title: Toro Military Socialism
events.description: After Chaco War, young officer Colonel David Toro launched coup, establishing 'military socialism' government. Toro government declared labor reforms, recognized unions, and in 1937 confiscated Standard Oil assets, Latin America's first oil nationalization. These reforms marked Bolivia's turn toward social revolution.

events.title: MNR Foundation
events.description: Víctor Paz Estenssoro and others founded Nationalist Revolutionary Movement (MNR), party mixing nationalism, anti-imperialism and social reform. MNR attracted middle class, miners and peasants. In 1943 MNR briefly participated in Villarroel government, but overthrown in 1946, leaders exiled. MNR became main force in 1952 revolution.

events.title: Civil War and Miners' Uprising
events.description: MNR launched armed uprising attempting to seize power, triggering brief but intense civil war. Miners and peasants supported MNR, but government forces eventually suppressed uprising. Hundreds died, MNR leaders exiled again. However uprising demonstrated popular desire for change, paving way for 1952 revolution.

events.title: Electoral Victory Denied
events.description: Exiled Paz Estenssoro won presidential election, MNR won congressional majority. But military refused to hand over power, launched coup, establishing military government. This angered people, leading to widespread protests and strikes. Military government couldn't maintain order, creating conditions for MNR revolution.

events.title: Revolutionary Reforms
events.description: MNR government implemented radical reforms: 1952 universal suffrage extended to illiterates (mainly Indians), voters increased from 200,000 to over 1 million; October 1952 nationalized three major tin companies, establishing Bolivian Mining Corporation (COMIBOL); 1953 land reform confiscated large estates, distributed land to peasants, abolished feudalism. These reforms fundamentally changed Bolivian social structure.

events.title: Land Reform
events.description: Paz Estenssoro signed land reform decree in Cochabamba, abolishing large estate system (latifundia), distributing land to peasants. 'Land to the tiller' became slogan. Labor servitude binding peasants abolished, hundreds of thousands of Quechua and Aymara peasants owned land for first time. Reform eliminated colonial-era feudal relations but also caused land fragmentation and agricultural productivity issues.

events.title: Economic Stabilization Plan
events.description: Facing hyperinflation and economic chaos, Paz government under US pressure implemented stabilization plan. Plan froze wages, cut government spending, accepted US aid. These measures stabilized economy but angered left and miners who saw this as revolution betrayal. MNR began splitting into right, center and left factions.

events.title: Barrientos Military Coup
events.description: Vice President General René Barrientos launched military coup, overthrowing Paz Estenssoro, ending MNR revolutionary period. Barrientos established pro-US military government, repressing left and miners' movement. Coup opened nearly 20 years of military dictatorship with violent repression and human rights violations.

events.title: San Juan Massacre
events.description: Army attacked miners and families celebrating San Juan festival in Siglo XX mining district, using machine guns and aircraft bombing. At least 87 died including women and children. Massacre aimed to crush radical miners' movement, becoming one of darkest events in Bolivian labor history. Barrientos government brutality sparked more resistance.

events.title: Che Guevara Captured and Killed
events.description: Cuban revolutionary Che Guevara led guerrilla warfare in Bolivia, attempting to ignite revolution. But guerrillas failed to gain peasant support, hunted by Bolivian army (with CIA assistance). Guevara captured in La Higuera village, executed next day. His death made him global revolutionary icon but also marked Bolivian guerrilla movement failure.

events.title: Leftist Military Governments
events.description: After Barrientos' death, Bolivia experienced brief leftist military government period. General Juan José Torres came to power in 1970, pursuing socialist policies, allowing worker participation in management, establishing relations with Cuba and USSR. Workers and students established People's Assembly. But Torres government lasted only one year, overthrown by right-wing coup in 1971.

events.title: Banzer Dictatorship
events.description: Colonel Hugo Banzer launched coup, establishing right-wing military dictatorship. Banzer government brutally repressed dissent, banned unions, censored media, tortured and killed opponents. But utilizing high tin prices in 1970s, economy grew. Banzer attempted to legitimize rule through 1978 elections, but election fraud obvious, triggering crisis.

events.title: Chaotic Democratic Transition
events.description: Bolivia descended into political chaos, experiencing 10 governments in just 4 years. Elections, coups and interim governments rotated. 1980's García Meza coup particularly brutal, called 'Cocaine Coup' for military government's deep involvement in drug trafficking. International pressure and economic collapse finally forced military to withdraw.

events.title: Democracy Restored
events.description: Military under pressure agreed to democratic transition. 1980 election winner Hernán Siles Zuazo (UDP coalition) finally assumed presidency, ending 18 years military rule. Bolivia began difficult democratic consolidation process. But Siles inherited severe economic crisis: hyperinflation, debt crisis, tin price collapse. His government struggled responding to crisis.

events.title: New Economic Policy
events.description: Paz Estenssoro elected president again (fourth time), implemented radical neoliberal 'New Economic Policy' (NPE). Policy included: tight monetary policy ending hyperinflation (annual inflation reached 24,000%), privatizing state enterprises, cutting government spending, opening markets. Policy successfully controlled inflation but caused massive unemployment, particularly state mining company laying off tens of thousands of miners. Social cost enormous.

events.title: Tin Price Collapse and Miners' Crisis
events.description: International tin price collapsed, Bolivian Mining Corporation near bankruptcy. Government closed many mines, dismissed about 23,000 miners. Mining communities collapsed, former miners moved to urban slums or coca growing areas. This ended miners' era as Bolivia's most important political force. Many former miners entered coca cultivation and cocaine trade.

events.title: Neoliberal Reform Period
events.description: Successive governments continued neoliberal policies: privatization (including oil, telecommunications, railways), multilateral free trade, foreign investment opening. Economy achieved low growth, macroeconomic stability, but inequality intensified. Most indigenous people and poor didn't benefit. Discontent with neoliberalism gradually accumulated, creating conditions for left-wing resurgence.

events.title: Indigenous Lowland March
events.description: Indigenous organizations from Beni organized 'March for Dignity and Territory,' walking 640 kilometers to La Paz, demanding land rights recognition and autonomy. March was milestone in Bolivian indigenous movement, bringing lowland indigenous peoples' (about 34 nations) demands to national attention. Government forced to acknowledge some demands. March opened new era of indigenous political mobilization.

events.title: Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada Reforms
events.description: President Sánchez de Lozada (Goni) implemented 'Popular Participation Law,' decentralizing to municipalities, recognizing indigenous communities. Education reform introduced bilingual education. Constitutional reform recognized Bolivia's multicultural and multiethnic nature. These reforms aimed to incorporate indigenous people into democratic system, but critics considered insufficient, reforms occurred within neoliberal framework.

events.title: Coca Eradication and US Drug War
events.description: Under US pressure, Banzer government pursued 'Dignity Plan,' forcibly eradicating 'surplus' coca cultivation in Chapare region. Military and police violently destroyed coca fields, arrested peasants. Coca growers (cocaleros) organized resistance, union led by Evo Morales became main opposition force. Eradication plan intensified conflict, making Morales national figure.

events.title: Cochabamba Water War
events.description: Cochabamba people uprising against water privatization. Government sold water system to US Bechtel company, causing water bills to skyrocket, poor couldn't afford. Tens of thousands protested, set up roadblocks, clashed with police. Government declared martial law but protests continued. Finally government canceled contract, Bechtel withdrew. Water War became symbolic victory for anti-neoliberal movement, inspiring nationwide resistance.

events.title: Gas War and Black October
events.description: Opposition to plan exporting natural gas through Chile triggered massive protests and roadblocks. Indigenous peoples, peasants and urban poor demanded gas nationalization. Government sent military to repress in El Alto, La Paz satellite city, killing about 60 protesters, mainly indigenous. 'Black October' massacre sparked national outrage, hundreds of thousands poured into La Paz demanding President Sánchez de Lozada resign. October 17 Goni fled by plane to US.

events.title: Second Gas War
events.description: Successor President Carlos Mesa faced new round of protests and roadblocks, demanding gas nationalization and constituent assembly. Mesa couldn't meet demands, forced to resign. His successor Rodríguez hastily called elections. Indigenous movement, unions and social organizations' mobilization reached peak, making neoliberal regime unsustainable. These 'Gas and Water Wars' paved way for left-wing victory.

events.title: Evo Morales Elected President
events.description: Aymara coca farmer leader Evo Morales elected president with 53.7% vote, first time in Bolivian democratic history someone won absolute majority in first round. Morales was Bolivia and South America's first indigenous president. His Movement for Socialism (MAS) party also won congress. Morales' victory represented indigenous and poor's historic rise, ending 500 years of colonial and white elite rule.

events.title: Constituent Assembly
events.description: Bolivia convened constituent assembly to draft new constitution. Assembly held in Sucre but highly politicized and conflictive. MAS and indigenous movement demanded profound change, right-wing opposition resisted. Assembly debated indigenous rights, land reform, autonomy and state structure. Eastern lowland provinces (Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando, Tarija) demanded autonomy, confronting central government.

events.title: Natural Gas Nationalization
events.description: Morales 100 days after inauguration announced gas nationalization, military occupied gas fields. Foreign companies required to renegotiate contracts, keeping more profits in Bolivia. Nationalization widely popular in Bolivia, achieving Gas and Water Wars' core demand. But raised concerns among foreign investors and neighbors (particularly Brazil). Nationalization increased government revenue, funding social programs.

events.title: Political Crisis and Recall Referendum
events.description: Opposition-controlled eastern provinces declared autonomy, confronting Morales government. Right-wing protests and violence attacked MAS supporters. August Morales and several governors faced recall referendum, Morales confirmed with 67% support. September 'Porvenir Massacre,' right-wing militia killed about 20 pro-government peasants. US ambassador accused of coordinating opposition, expelled. Crisis pushed Bolivia toward civil war brink.

events.title: New Constitution
events.description: New constitution passed in referendum with 61.4%. Constitution defined Bolivia as 'Plurinational State' (Estado Plurinacional), recognizing rights, languages and autonomy of 36 indigenous nations. Constitution recognized rights of Mother Earth (Pachamama), limited land ownership, allowed presidential reelection once, expanded state control over economy. New constitution was one of Latin America's most progressive, representing symbolic break with colonial legacy.

events.title: Morales Reelection
events.description: In first election under new constitution, Morales reelected with 64% vote, MAS won two-thirds congressional majority. Victory consolidated 'Democratic Cultural Revolution Process.' Commodity boom (particularly gas and minerals) provided government funding for social programs, reducing poverty. Morales internationally became symbol of left-wing and indigenous rights.

events.title: Economic Growth and Social Programs
events.description: Bolivia experienced significant economic growth in 2010s, GDP growing about 4-5% annually, one of South America's best-performing economies. Government implemented social programs: elderly pension (Renta Dignidad), child subsidy (Bono Juancito Pinto), maternity subsidy. Poverty rate fell from 60% in 2005 to about 34% in 2018. But economy still depended on raw material exports, failing to diversify.

events.title: TIPNIS Conflict
events.description: Government plan to build highway through TIPNIS (Isiboro Sécure National Park and Indigenous Territory) sparked lowland indigenous and environmentalist protests. Police violently repressed peaceful march, drawing national condemnation. Conflict exposed Morales government internal contradictions: developmentalism vs environmental protection, highland vs lowland indigenous interests. Government finally canceled highway but image damaged.

events.title: Morales Third Election
events.description: Morales elected president third time with 61% vote, his third consecutive victory. MAS maintained congressional majority. Victory based on economic growth, social program success and opposition division. But critics accused Morales of authoritarian tendencies, corruption and personality cult. Middle class and urban voters began alienating.

events.title: Reelection Referendum Failed
events.description: Morales sought constitutional amendment to remove presidential term limits for 2019 reelection bid. But constitutional referendum 51.3% voted against. This was Morales' first electoral defeat. But 2017 Constitutional Court (viewed as pro-government) ruled term limits violated human rights, allowing Morales to run indefinitely, sparking controversy.

events.title: Election Dispute and Political Crisis
events.description: October 20 general election, Morales claimed first-round victory. But vote counting suddenly interrupted for 24 hours, after resumption Morales vote surged, exceeding 10% margin needed to avoid runoff. Opposition and electoral observers (including OAS) alleged election fraud. Massive protests erupted, police and military refused to repress. November 10 military commander suggested Morales resign, Morales, vice president and congressional leaders resigned, fleeing to Mexico.

events.title: Áñez Interim Government
events.description: Senate Vice President Jeanine Áñez declared herself interim president, filling power vacuum in constitutional order chaos. Áñez was right-wing conservative, promising to call new elections. But her government immediately sparked controversy: repressing MAS supporters, killing about 36 protesters at Senkata and Sacaba, persecuting former government officials. Morales and MAS called this coup.

events.title: MAS Returns to Power
events.description: After multiple delays, October 18 held new elections. MAS candidate Luis Arce (Morales' former economy minister) won 55% first-round vote, overwhelming victory. MAS regained congressional control. Result confirmed MAS popular base despite Morales controversy. Áñez conceded defeat, Arce inaugurated November 8. Bolivia avoided civil war, democratic institutions tested.

events.title: Arce Government and Economic Challenges
events.description: Arce government struggled to restore stability, facing COVID-19 pandemic, economic recession and political polarization. Government dealt with 2020 crisis legacy, prosecuting Áñez government members. MAS internally split, Morales returned from Argentina, attempted to control party, tensions with Arce. Economy faced foreign exchange shortages, fuel shortages and declining international reserves.

events.title: Morales and Arce Split
events.description: MAS publicly split into two factions: supporting Morales (hoping to run again in 2025) and supporting Arce (seeking reelection). Split weakened left, possibly providing right-wing resurgence opportunity. Legal issues plagued Morales (including allegations of relationships with minors). Both factions competed for party control and 2025 presidential candidacy.

events.title: Contemporary Bolivia Challenges
events.description: Bolivia remains one of Latin America's poorest countries despite recent progress. Nation faces multiple challenges: economy heavily dependent on gas and mineral exports, climate change threats (glacier melting, droughts), persistent racial and regional divisions, corruption, drug trafficking. Politics highly polarized, MAS left vs right-wing opposition, also MAS internally split. Bolivia still demands Chile restore sea access but negotiations fruitless. Nevertheless, Bolivia's indigenous movement and plurinational state experiment sets example for global indigenous rights. Bolivian culture rich, preserving Aymara and Quechua traditions, Andean music and textile arts world-renowned. Carnivals (particularly Oruro Carnival, World Heritage listed) showcase cultural mixing. Bolivia's future depends on overcoming divisions, achieving inclusive development, protecting environmental and cultural heritage.
